phonemes.desc: Long open-mid back [ɔː] with acute marking stress and length; the name derives from *Wōđanaz, 'the furious'
Voiced dental fricative [ð], the eth; it replaced Proto-Germanic *đ and gives the name its Norse colour
Short close front [i] and alveolar nasal [n]; the participial/derivative suffix
Final alveolar nasal [n], geminated in Old Norse orthography as nn

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-thin' — hold the first vowel long like 'awe', then a soft 'th' as in 'this', and a crisp 'nin'.

pronunciation.note: Óðinn is Tier 1: the acute on Ó marks stress and length on the first syllable, and together with the distinctive letter ð these are features the ASCII form loses. The name descends from *Wōđanaz; the initial w- was lost in West Norse, giving Óðinn rather than *Wóðinn.

domains.title: Wisdom, War, Death, Poetry
domains.subtitle: The domain of Óðinn
domains.lead: In the norse tradition, Óðinn is the Allfather: god of the battle-slain and of the mead of poetry, of wisdom bought at any price. Where Þórr defends the world with his hammer, Óðinn wanders it in a broad-brimmed hat and grey cloak, trading eyes, hanging on trees, and outwitting giants to know what is coming.

cards.name: Hávamál Sacrifice
cards.desc: Óðinn hung nine nights on Yggdrasill, pierced by a spear, to seize the runes in an act of self-willed death.

cards.name: Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: He stole the fermented mead of inspiration from the giant Suttungr and carried it back to Ásgarðr in his belly.

cards.name: Valkyries
cards.desc: His shield-maidens choose the slain and bear the worthy to Valhöll, the hall of the battle-dead.

cards.name: Runes and Revelation
cards.desc: Óðinn's ceaseless quest for wisdom drives him to summon dead seeresses, bargain with Mímir, and read fate itself.

mythology.lead: Óðinn is the most restless of the Æsir: a war-god who wins by wit, a poet who stole his art, a seeker who paid an eye and nine nights on a tree for wisdom the gods did not hand him. His myths are all bargains — with seeresses, giants, and his own body — and all of them end in knowledge, victory, or the foreknowledge of defeat.

myths.title: The Hanging on the Windy Tree
myths.text:
In Hávamál 138, Óðinn speaks of a sacrifice 'to myself, to myself': he hung nine nights on the windy tree — the stanza does not name it; later tradition identifies it with Yggdrasill — pierced by a spear, given neither bread nor drinking horn. From that ordeal he seized the runes, the letters of power that carry knowledge, healing, and sorcery through the worlds.

The passage is one of the most striking shamanic initiations in European literature. Óðinn does not receive wisdom as a gift; he wins it by dying in a controlled way, suspended between worlds. The gallows and the spear become his ritual tools, and the tree becomes the axis along which the initiate ascends.

myths.title: The Seeress's Vision
myths.text:
Óðinn summons a dead völva and compels her to answer his questions about the origins of the world and the coming doom. She tells him of the golden age of the gods, the murder of Ymir, the creation of dwarves, and finally of Ragnarǫk: the wolf Fenrir's release, the serpent's rising, the darkening of the sun, and the fall of the gods.

The poem dramatizes Óðinn's defining obsession: he already knows much, yet he cannot stop seeking more. Even foreknowledge does not grant escape. The myth presents him as a king who pays for wisdom with the anxiety of certainty, a god who knows precisely how his reign will end.

myths.title: The Eye in the Well of Mímir
myths.text:
Beneath one root of Yggdrasill lies Mímir's well, in which wisdom and understanding are hidden, and Mímir is its keeper. Óðinn came to the well and asked for a single drink; the price was an eye. He pledged it, and Mímir took the eye and cast it into the well, where it still lies — so Snorri tells in Gylfaginning 15 — and ever after Óðinn sees with one eye in this world while his other gazes into the water of hidden things. The bargain outlived its broker: when the Vanir sent Mímir's severed head to the Æsir, Óðinn embalmed it with herbs and spoke charms over it until the head spoke and revealed what is hidden, and he consults it still.

The myth is the theology of Óðinn in miniature: vision is bought with vision, and the god's famous one-eyed gaze is the visible ledger of his trade. What Mímir's well sees, Óðinn need not guess — and what it cost him is written on his face.

myths.title: The Mead of Poetry
myths.text:
Poetry in the Norse world had a body and a price. When the Æsir and Vanir made peace, they spat into a vat, and from the spittle they fashioned Kvasir, the wisest of beings — whom two dwarves murdered, whose blood they mixed with honey and brewed into the mead Óðrerir in three vessels, Óðrerir, Són, and Boðn. The giant Suttungr seized the mead and set his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it inside a mountain. Óðinn bored into the rock as a snake, spent three nights with the giantess, drank all three vessels dry, and flew out as an eagle with Suttungr behind him in eagle form; he vomited the mead into the vats of the gods at Ásgarðr, losing a few drops backwards — Snorri's explanation, in Skáldskaparmál, for why bad poets exist.

The story makes poetry an intoxicant literally stolen from death: the mead is brewed from a murdered sage, carried in a god's belly, and decanted with some drops gone sour. Every skald who praised a king was drinking Óðrerir — and, as the myth insists, some of what reaches any poet is what fell backwards.

lore.syncretism: Interpretatio romana named him Mercury: Tacitus (Germania 9) reports that Mercury is the chief god of the Germani, and the equation stuck — the dies Mercurii became Wednesday in English, Wodanstag in Dutch, and Óðinsdagr in Iceland. Anglo-Saxon royal houses claimed descent from Woden, and the genealogies of Wessex and Mercia trace their lines back to him — a pagan ancestor quietly retained by Christian kings. On the continent he rides at the head of the Wild Hunt, the Wodanes her, and medieval German folklore kept him as leader of the furious host. His deeper kin are debated: the one-eyed wanderer, the hanged god, the lord of ecstasy — his very name, from *wōđanaz, means 'the furious, the possessed' — invite, and resist, comparison with Lugus, Rudra, and the shamans of the northern world. Wagner's Wotan, made brooding and self-doubting in the Ring, and Marvel's Odin, made cosmic and paternal, are the two great modern masks of the Allfather.
lore.culturalLegacy: Óðinn is the best-known Norse god in the modern world. Wednesday still carries his name; place-names from Odense in Denmark to Wansdyke in England mark the roads and boundaries his cult once blessed. The Viking-Age revival of the nineteenth century and the Ásatrú movement of the twentieth restored his worship, controversially, to living religion. In mass culture he appears as Marvel's one-eyed Allfather, as Gandalf — Tolkien's wandering grey pilgrim owes him a clear debt — and as Wagner's Wotan. The runes he won hang from necks as jewellery; the valknut, his triple knot, appears on tattoos worldwide. Few pagan gods have travelled so far from their ninth-century hearths with so much of their complexity intact.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Óðinn is the myth of intelligence as sacrifice. Every god in the Eddas has power; only Óðinn has invoices. He gives an eye for a drink from Mímir's well, nine nights on a spear-pierced tree for the runes, his dignity as a god for three nights as a snake in a giant's mountain — and what he buys is always the same commodity: to know. The Hávamál hanging makes the transaction explicit: I know that I hung on a wind-wracked tree nine whole nights, wounded by a spear, given to Óðinn, myself to myself — the only god in the corpus whose central ritual is a death he performs upon himself.

What the myth knows, and says plainly, is the price of that knowledge: Óðinn is the god who foresees Ragnarǫk and cannot prevent it. He trades happiness for certainty and calls the trade wisdom. In an information age that runs on the same bargain — everything knowable, nothing unknown, serenity sold for data — the one-eyed god is less an antique than a diagnosis.

lore.archaeology: Adam of Bremen describes the great temple at Uppsala (c. 1070s), where Óðinn was honored alongside Þórr and Freyr. The Rök runestone (Ög 136) memorializes the dead Vémóðr in riddling, eschatological stanzas; the Torslunda plate depicts a one-eyed dancer often identified with Óðinn. Valkyrie pendants and spear-god silver figurines from sites such as Lunda and Uppåkra point to his warrior cult.
